items.explanation: Drafted by John Dickinson and adopted in July 1775, the petition professed loyalty and begged George III to broker a reconciliation — the king refused even to receive it.
options: A. To rally the colonies for war with Britain
B. To seek redress of colonial economic grievances
C. To ask the king to arrange a reconciliation
D. To request American independence
items.stem: The purpose of the Olive Branch Petition (1775) was to

option_explanations.A: The petition did not rally the colonies for war. It did the opposite, professing loyalty to the king even as fighting had begun at Lexington and Concord.
option_explanations.B: The petition did mention grievances, but its purpose — its actual request of the king — was to arrange a reconciliation between Britain and the colonies, not merely to fix economic complaints.
option_explanations.C: Correct. Drafted by John Dickinson and adopted in July 1775, the Olive Branch Petition professed loyalty and begged George III to broker a reconciliation — the king refused even to receive it.
option_explanations.D: The petition did not request independence. It affirmed loyalty to the crown; independence would not be declared for another year.

items.explanation: London expected a quick win, but commanders like Howe and Burgoyne proved ordinary, while Loyalist support, colonial disunity, and the Royal Navy's limits all disappointed British planners.
options: A. They expected their generals to win easily
B. Loyalists were numerous throughout the colonies
C. The Continental Army lacked discipline
D. The Royal Navy was unmatched
items.stem: At the war's outset, British confidence rested on all of the following EXCEPT

option_explanations.A: Correct — this is the exception. British confidence rested on Loyalist numbers, colonial disunity, and the Royal Navy, not on brilliant generalship: commanders like Howe and Burgoyne proved ordinary, and Washington matched them in the field.
option_explanations.B: Loyalists were a real basis of British confidence: perhaps a fifth to a third of colonists remained loyal to the crown, a substantial internal base.
option_explanations.C: The Continental Army's lack of discipline was a real basis of British confidence: at the war's outset it was a raw, untrained force next to professional British regulars.
option_explanations.D: The Royal Navy's supremacy was a real basis of British confidence: it was unmatched in the world and could blockade, transport troops, and bombard coastal towns.

items.explanation: The 1783 treaty recognized independence and granted the trans-Appalachian west, but Canada remained British and Loyalists were promised a chance to recover confiscated property.
options: A. The west beyond the Appalachians went to the Americans
B. Britain recognized American independence
C. Quebec and its surroundings were ceded to the Americans
D. Loyalists could seek return of seized property
items.stem: All of the following were in the Treaty of Paris of 1783 EXCEPT

option_explanations.A: This was in the treaty: Britain ceded the trans-Appalachian west, with the Mississippi as the new nation's western boundary.
option_explanations.B: This was in the treaty: Britain formally recognized the independence of the United States.
option_explanations.C: Correct — this is the exception. Quebec and Canada were not ceded; they remained British, and the new United States–Canadian boundary ran along the Great Lakes.
option_explanations.D: This was in the treaty: Article V provided that Loyalists could seek the return of confiscated property through the state courts.

items.explanation: With husbands and sons at war, women ran farms, shops, and estates — keeping the colonial economy functioning — while also sewing, nursing, and in cases like Molly Pitcher serving on the battlefield.
options: A. They financed much of the colonial cause
B. They wrote pro-resistance newspaper essays
C. They clothed the freezing troops at Valley Forge
D. They kept households and businesses running during the war
items.stem: Women contributed vitally to the war effort because they

option_explanations.A: Women did not finance the colonial cause. The war was financed by French loans, foreign aid, and Congress's paper money — not by women's wealth.
option_explanations.B: Some women did write for the cause, but essays were not the vital contribution. The indispensable work was economic: keeping farms and businesses running.
option_explanations.C: Women did sew and knit for soldiers, but 'clothing the freezing troops at Valley Forge' overstates one episode. The vital, war-sustaining contribution was keeping the economy functioning.
option_explanations.D: Correct. With husbands and sons at war, women ran farms, shops, and estates — keeping the colonial economy functioning — while also nursing, sewing, and in cases like Molly Pitcher serving on the battlefield.

items.explanation: Congress under the Articles could not tax, regulate commerce, or compel states to provide troops — it could only request them, leaving the national government nearly powerless.
options: A. Settle disputes between states
B. Raise an army
C. Conduct foreign relations
D. Print money
items.stem: The weakness of the national government under the Articles of Confederation was shown by its inability to

option_explanations.A: Congress could settle disputes between states under the Articles — it had that power. Its crippling weakness was the inability to compel states to do anything.
option_explanations.B: Correct. Under the Articles, Congress could not tax and could not draft soldiers; it could only request troops and money from the states, which often refused — leaving the national government nearly powerless.
option_explanations.C: Congress could conduct foreign relations under the Articles — it negotiated the Treaty of Paris of 1783. The weakness was in domestic enforcement, not diplomacy.
option_explanations.D: Congress could print money under the Articles — it issued Continentals. The problem was that it could not tax to give that money value, so it depreciated into worthlessness.

items.explanation: The 'insurgents' were western Massachusetts farmers crushed by debt and taxes after the Revolution -- men like Daniel Shays, a former Continental Army captain. Courts were foreclosing their farms, and the rebels shut the courts down by force. Washington's alarm was about indebted agrarians, not foreign agents, merchants, or the enslaved.
options: A. Debt-burdened farmers of western Massachusetts
B. British agents provocateurs sent to stir disorder
C. Urban merchants protesting trade restrictions
D. Enslaved people rising for their freedom
items.stem: The 'insurgents' Washington describes in the letter were primarily
items.stimulus:
The following questions refer to the excerpt below.

"I feel myself exceedingly obliged to you for the full & friendly communications in your letters... Commotions of this sort, like snow-balls, gather strength as they roll, if there is no opposition in the way to divide and crumble them."
—George Washington to Henry Knox on Shays's Rebellion, 1786 (abridged)

option_explanations.A: Correct. The 'insurgents' were debt-burdened farmers of western Massachusetts — men like Daniel Shays, a former Continental Army captain — whose farms were being foreclosed by courts enforcing debts and taxes. They shut the courts down by force.
option_explanations.B: No British agents were behind the uprising. Shays's Rebellion was a homegrown revolt of indebted American farmers against their own state government.
option_explanations.C: Urban merchants were on the other side: they favored the courts and creditors and wanted the rebellion suppressed, not the rebels' aims advanced.
option_explanations.D: The insurgents were not enslaved people. They were free white farmers protesting debt foreclosures and high taxes.

items.explanation: The specter of Shays haunted Philadelphia: the Constitution gave Congress power to tax, raise armies, and call forth the militia 'to execute the Laws of the Union, suppress Insurrections and repel Invasions.' Washington wanted energy in government, not a bill of rights for rebellion, disarmament, or the Articles' unanimity rule.
options: A. A bill of rights guaranteeing the right of rebellion
B. The prohibition of any national standing army
C. A federal government strong enough to tax, raise armies, and suppress insurrections
D. The requirement of unanimous state consent for federal action
items.stem: The fear Washington expresses in the letter most directly shaped which feature of the new Constitution?
items.stimulus:
The following questions refer to the excerpt below.

"I feel myself exceedingly obliged to you for the full & friendly communications in your letters... Commotions of this sort, like snow-balls, gather strength as they roll, if there is no opposition in the way to divide and crumble them."
—George Washington to Henry Knox on Shays's Rebellion, 1786 (abridged)

option_explanations.A: The Constitution contains no bill of rights guaranteeing rebellion, and Washington was alarmed by the rebellion, not sympathetic to a right of revolt. The Bill of Rights came later, in 1791.
option_explanations.B: Washington wanted the opposite of banning a standing army. The Constitution authorized Congress to raise and support armies — the very power the Articles had lacked.
option_explanations.C: Correct. The specter of Shays haunted Philadelphia: the Constitution gave the federal government power to tax, raise armies, and call forth the militia to 'suppress Insurrections' — a government with energy enough to enforce its laws.
option_explanations.D: Unanimous state consent was the Articles' rule — the very paralysis the framers were escaping. The Constitution replaced it with ratification by nine states and majority rule in Congress.

items.explanation: Washington's logic -- 'If government shrinks, or is unable to enforce its laws... anarchy and confusion must prevail' -- points to one remedy: a government with the power to compel obedience. He did not counsel appeasement, abolishing the states, or appealing to Britain.
options: A. Appeasing the insurgents by granting their demands
B. A government strong enough to enforce its laws
C. Disbanding the state governments entirely
D. Appealing to Britain for military assistance

"I feel myself exceedingly obliged to you for the full & friendly communications in your letters... Commotions of this sort, like snow-balls, gather strength as they roll, if there is no opposition in the way to divide and crumble them."
—George Washington to Henry Knox on Shays's Rebellion, 1786 (abridged)

option_explanations.A: Washington did not counsel appeasing the insurgents. His letter treats the rebellion as a dangerous 'commotion' that must be opposed, not a set of demands to be granted.
option_explanations.B: Correct. Washington's logic — that commotions 'gather strength as they roll, if there is no opposition in the way' — points to one remedy: a government strong enough to enforce its laws.
option_explanations.C: Washington proposed nothing like disbanding the state governments. His concern was the weakness of the national government under the Articles, not the existence of the states.
option_explanations.D: Washington did not suggest appealing to Britain for help. The remedy he envisioned was American: a stronger national government of the Americans' own making.
